tei:titleStmt.tei:title: Six Questions for the Seder Night, as recalled by Paul Christian Kirchner in his Jüdisches Ceremoniel (Nuremberg, 1717)

tei:div.tei:head: Six Questions for the Seder Night, as recalled by Paul Christian Kirchner in his Jüdisches Ceremoniel (Nuremberg, 1717)

tei:l.tei:note: After drinking from [the first cup], he takes the bottom loaf from the first night, Israel, and breaks it in half, and wraps half of it in a clean handtowel, and hangs it over his shoulders, as if one were about to travel, and says:

tei:lg.tei:l: “Hear ye, children! This is how our ancestors hastily, carrying a staff and unleavened dough, went out from the hand of Pharaoh.”
1.) The eldest of the sons asks: “Father, why did they go out then, as you showed us?”

After which the father answers: “Pharaoh oppressed us with hard labor, gave us water and bread, but without water. But after God showed us grace and allowed us to be led out by Moses, each of us took dough on his shoulders and left Egypt with it.”
2.) The son asks: “Why do we eat the green of the radish, along with the apples, nuts, and cinnamon?”
The father replies: “Our parents had to chop straw under plaster all day, and the green of the horseradish represents the straw, the other part the plaster.”
3.) [The son asks:] “Then why do we eat the horseradish?”
The father answers: “The work came bitterly upon us, as did the bread, so we eat horseradish.”
4.) [The son asks:] “Why do we eat parsley dipped in saltwater or vinegar?”
The father says: “Because back then we had nothing to eat but grass, which we dressed with vinegar.”
5.) [The son asks:] “Why do we eat eggs?”

After which the father answers: “When one of our ancestors died, we would not be allowed to cook on that same day; instead, strangers sent us a little white bread, ashes, and eggs, and we would commemorate the bloody sour and arduous death-work.”
6.) [The son asks:] “Why is there a piece of roasted meat upon the dish?”
[The father answers:] “Because the paschal lamb was usually roasted.”

tei:note.tei:p: The loaves are referred to in the Jüdisches Ceremoniel as Chan (Kohen), Levi, and Israel. Note that in modern practice the middle matzo is broken, not the bottom one. This is likely a misremembering on the part of Kirchner.
Note that the Four Questions are traditionally recited by the youngest son. This is likely another misremembering on the part of Kirchner.

Literally: “Easter lamb.” Uncommon in modern German usage, at the time both Passover and Easter were referred to as such. This is still the case in many languages — see Greek Πάσχα των Ιουδαίων, French Pâque juive, Finnish juutalainen pääsiäinen, and Spanish pascua de los judíos. Note, though, that in all three of those languages, the word for Easter derives from the Hebrew פֶּסַח via Aramaic, which is not the case in German — or in English.
